quote: Has none but returned to give thanks to God?
firstReading: Paul directs Titus to form Christians in a public holiness marked by readiness for every good work, respect for legitimate authority, gentleness, and freedom from contentious speech. This conduct rests not on any claim of self-made righteousness but on God’s mercy. Through the saving kindness of God our Savior, believers are washed in rebirth and renewed by the Holy Spirit, poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that, justified by grace, they become heirs of eternal life.
psalmSummary: Psalm 23 confesses the Lord as the shepherd who personally provides for his people. He gives rest, leads them to life-giving waters, restores their strength, and guides them along right paths for the honor of his name. Even in the dark valley, the faithful need not fear because his protecting presence remains near. The psalm culminates in grateful confidence: divine goodness and mercy pursue the believer, whose true dwelling is with the Lord.
gospelSummary: As Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, ten lepers call to him from a distance and beg for mercy. He sends them to show themselves to the priests, in accordance with the restoration required by the law, and they are cleansed while going. Yet only one turns back, glorifying God and falling at Jesus’ feet in thanksgiving. He is a Samaritan, an outsider in the eyes of many. Jesus asks where the other nine are and declares that this man’s faith has saved him. The Gospel distinguishes bodily healing from the fuller salvation received in faith-filled gratitude and worship.
saintReflection: Saint Martin of Tours (Memorial): Saint Martin of Tours (c. 316–397) entered military service as a young catechumen and became renowned for cutting his cloak to share it with a poorly clothed man. A vision of Christ wearing the garment deepened his recognition of the Lord in the needy. After baptism Martin embraced monastic life, studied under Saint Hilary of Poitiers, and was later chosen Bishop of Tours. He combined prayer, pastoral visitation, evangelization, and care for the poor, while opposing the use of civil execution against those accused of heresy. Martin's life teaches that mercy toward a neighbor is service to Christ and that truth must not be defended through cruelty. He invites simplicity, peacemaking, generous almsgiving, prayer for enemies, and pastoral authority conformed to the gentleness of the Good Shepherd.
dailyPrayer:
Lord Jesus Christ, source of mercy and giver of salvation, teach us to recognize every grace as a gift from the Father. Cleanse us from sin, renew us by the Holy Spirit, and make our lives a continual return to you in thanksgiving. Preserve us from harsh speech, quarrels, pride, and the false belief that we have saved ourselves.

Through the intercession of Saint Martin of Tours, give us hearts attentive to those who are poor, afflicted, excluded, or forgotten. May we serve you in them with reverence and generosity. Make us lovers of peace, steadfast in truth, and unwilling to answer error or injury with cruelty. Strengthen pastors to shepherd your people with prayerful gentleness, and teach all the baptized to walk in the paths of righteousness.

Good Shepherd, remain with us in every shadowed valley. Lead us beside the waters of life, restore our souls, and bring us at last into the dwelling place of your mercy. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
The readings reveal salvation as God’s merciful initiative, received in faith and expressed through grateful, gentle, and charitable lives. Titus rejects every boast in human righteousness: baptismal rebirth and renewal in the Holy Spirit come from the kindness of God through Jesus Christ. The Christian therefore does good not to earn divine mercy, but because grace has made him or her an heir of eternal life.

The Samaritan leper embodies this response. Cleansed on the way, he returns to Jesus, gives glory to God, and prostrates himself in thanksgiving. His return discloses that salvation is more than relief from suffering; it is communion with Christ in worshiping faith. Psalm 23 gives this communion its pastoral form: the Lord guides, restores, protects, and welcomes his people into his house.

Saint Martin’s mercy toward the needy reflects this same Gospel vision. His life directs believers to recognize Christ in the neighbor and to let pastoral care bear the likeness of the Good Shepherd. Truth, mercy, prayer, peace, and gratitude belong together because all flow from the grace of the Savior.
exegesis:
Context: Titus 3:1-7 joins Christian moral witness to the prior gift of salvation. Paul calls the community to be submissive to rulers and authorities, ready for good works, respectful in speech, peaceable, and gentle toward all. These commands do not authorize servility before injustice or silence before evil; rather, they describe a people whose conduct manifests the peace bestowed by Christ. Paul grounds this exhortation in humility. Christians remember that they too were once led astray and enslaved by disordered desires. No disciple may treat another with contempt, because every conversion begins in the mercy of God.

Context: The center of the passage is God’s saving kindness. Believers are not saved because they have performed righteous works capable of placing God under obligation. They are saved according to divine mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal in the Holy Spirit. The Church hears here an unmistakable baptismal horizon: through Christ, the Spirit is lavishly poured out, and the baptized are justified by grace. This grace makes them heirs in hope of eternal life. Good works remain necessary as the fruit and public shape of a life received from God; they are not a rival source of salvation.

Psalm: Psalm 23 answers this proclamation with trust. The Lord is not merely a guide who gives directions from afar; he is the shepherd whose own presence sustains the sheep. Green pastures, restful waters, and restored strength portray God’s tender care for the whole person. Right paths are paths ordered to the honor of God’s name, not routes chosen by self-will. The valley of darkness does not cease to be dark, but fear is overcome by the shepherd’s nearness. The table, anointing, and overflowing cup culminate in communion under God’s generous protection. The psalm thus teaches the baptized to receive life as a gift and to dwell in gratitude before the Lord.

Gospel: Luke places the healing of the ten lepers on Jesus’ journey toward Jerusalem. The lepers remain at a distance, reflecting the painful separation imposed by their condition, yet they recognize Jesus as master and appeal for mercy. Jesus instructs them to show themselves to the priests. Their obedience is itself an act of trust, for they set out before the healing is visible. As they go, all ten are cleansed. The priests would be able to verify their restoration and their return to communal worship. Jesus’ mercy therefore restores not only bodily health but also access to the life of the people.

Gospel: One healed man turns back. Luke emphasizes that he glorifies God, falls at Jesus’ feet, and gives thanks. These actions are worshipful and reveal where God’s saving work is encountered: in Jesus himself. The man is a Samaritan, someone regarded as religiously and socially suspect by many Jews. His status sharpens the Gospel’s question. The outsider recognizes and celebrates the gift, while the nine who also received cleansing do not return. Jesus does not deny their healing, but he announces a deeper blessing to the thankful Samaritan: his faith has saved him. Gratitude is not a decorative sentiment added after grace; it is faith’s return to the Giver, opening the healed person to the fullness of salvation.

Saints: Saint Martin of Tours gives a fitting witness to this pattern of mercy and recognition. As a catechumen, he shared part of his cloak with a poorly clothed man; the later vision of Christ wearing that garment deepened his recognition of the Lord in the needy. This tradition harmonizes with the Gospel’s summons to see divine mercy not as an abstraction but as a summons to reverent love. Martin’s later monastic life, formation under Saint Hilary of Poitiers, episcopal service, evangelization, and care for the poor show a shepherding ministry shaped by prayer. His opposition to civil execution for those accused of heresy also testifies that Christian truth cannot be defended by cruelty. The Good Shepherd guides with truth and protects with mercy.

Today: These readings call the Church to return to Christ with thanksgiving for baptismal grace. The question is not whether God has acted mercifully, but whether those who have received mercy give glory to him in worship and in their treatment of others. Titus makes this concrete through gentleness, peace, and readiness for good works. Psalm 23 anchors such conduct in confidence that the Lord himself provides and leads. The Samaritan teaches that faith approaches Jesus in grateful adoration. Saint Martin teaches that this adoration bears fruit in almsgiving, prayer, pastoral charity, and peacemaking. Christians may therefore ask for the grace to receive salvation humbly, to recognize Christ in the afflicted, and to let mercy govern both witness to truth and care for every neighbor.
